title: Features of a normal distribution
log: 2026-10-29T12:22:38Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: The existing normal distribution point is about how the mean and standard deviation set the centre and spread, with the 68–95–99.7 rule, while the new point covers only the bell shape, symmetry and equal mean, median and mode, so it is a narrower idea and not the same.

draft.title: Features of a normal distribution
card: A normal distribution is shaped like a bell. It has one peak in the middle, and the curve falls away on both sides.
It is symmetric. The left half is a mirror image of the right half, so the centre splits the data into two matching halves.
The mean, median and mode are all equal, and they sit at the peak. For example, if the mean mark is 60, the median and mode are also 60.
Scores near the centre are common. Scores far from the centre, in either tail, are rare.
draft.remember: A normal distribution is a symmetric bell with the mean, median and mode all at the centre.

a.q: The heights of a large group of students follow a normal distribution with a mean of 168 cm. What is the median height?
opts: It cannot be found without the range
a.why: In a normal distribution the mean and median are equal, so the median is 168 cm. The distribution is symmetric, so the median is not pulled to either side of the mean.
a.clue: Which measures of centre are equal in a normal distribution?

b.q: The weights of apples from an orchard in Orange follow a normal distribution. Which description of the graph is correct?
opts: Symmetric, with a single peak at the mean
Skewed right, with a long tail of heavy apples
Flat, with every weight equally likely
Symmetric, with two peaks either side of the mean
b.why: A normal distribution is a symmetric bell with one peak at the mean. A long tail on one side would mean the distribution is skewed, and two peaks would not be a bell shape.
b.clue: Think of the shape of a bell, with the peak at the centre.

b.best: Symmetric, with a single peak at the mean
